content: Pathology is a specialized branch of medicine that focuses on diagnosing diseases by examining organs, tissues, and cells at the gross, microscopic, and molecular levels. Physicians who practice pathology are often trained in both anatomical pathology and clinical pathology. Anatomical pathology involves the study of tissues and cells to diagnose diseases, while clinical pathology focuses on diagnosing diseases through laboratory analysis of bodily fluids. Anatomical pathologists use various techniques to examine tissues and cells. This includes gross examination, where diseased tissues are inspected with the naked eye, often aided by magnifying tools or stereomicroscopes for detailed analysis, especially in cases involving parasitic organisms. Histopathology involves the microscopic examination of stained tissue sections using histological techniques, with hematoxylin and eosin being the standard stains. Immunohistochemistry employs antibodies to detect specific proteins, aiding in distinguishing between disorders with similar appearances and characterizing molecular properties of cancers. In situ hybridization identifies specific DNA or RNA molecules in tissue sections, with fluorescent labeling (FISH) being a common method. Cytopathology examines loose cells spread on slides, while electron microscopy provides high magnification to visualize cellular organelles, though its use has been largely replaced by immunohistochemistry for many applications. Tissue cytogenetics visualizes chromosomes to identify genetic defects, and flow immunophenotyping uses flow cytometry to determine the immunophenotype of cells, particularly useful in diagnosing leukemia and lymphoma. Anatomical pathology encompasses several sub-disciplines. Surgical pathology is the most significant and time-intensive area, involving the examination of surgical specimens and biopsies. Cytopathology focuses on the microscopic examination of individual cells obtained from smears or fine-needle aspirations, with cytopathologists often providing immediate diagnoses during procedures. Molecular pathology is an emerging field that uses nucleic acid-based techniques, such as in situ hybridization and reverse-transcriptase polymerase chain reaction, to study diseases at the molecular level. Autopsy pathology involves determining disease factors contributing to death, with autopsies playing a role in medical education and quality assurance. Forensic pathology specializes in determining the cause of death and other legally relevant information, often in cases of non-medical or criminal circumstances. Training and certification for anatomical pathologists vary by country. In the United States, certification in anatomical pathology requires four years of medical school followed by three years of residency training. Many pathologists pursue additional fellowship training in subspecialties. In Canada, certification requires four years of medical school and five years of residency training, with further fellowship training common for subspecialization. Anatomical pathologists practice in various settings. In academic settings, they often combine diagnostic work with research, teaching, and training responsibilities. In private practice, group practices are common, where senior pathologists manage partnerships that contract with hospitals and clinicians. Large corporate providers of anatomical pathology services, such as AmeriPath in the United States, employ pathologists and offer economies of scale and specialized testing. Multispecialty groups, which include clinicians from various specialties, may employ pathologists to provide diagnostic services, sometimes owning their own laboratories or leasing space in controversial pod labs. Proposed changes to Medicare regulations may impact such arrangements in the United States.
